World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Do acupuncture and herbs actually help with menopause symptoms?
World.content:
Hot flushes, night sweats or swinging mood changes are some of the most common symptoms of menopause — the stage of a woman's life when menstrual periods stop permanently, and she is no longer fertile.

Some women choose to ride out the symptoms. Some choose hormone replacement therapy (HRT), also known as menopausal hormone therapy or MHT. This contains oestrogen, progesterone or combined therapies. Others use complementary therapies.

But do complementary therapies such as acupuncture and herbal medicines actually help?

Remind me, what's going on with menopause?

Menopause is a normal part of aging, as is the menopausal transition (or perimenopause), which occurs for several years before it. Some women's periods stop earlier than others. But most women become menopausal naturally between the ages of 45 and 55.

During menopause, women often have a range of symptoms. These can include hot flushes, night sweats, mood swings, joint discomfort, sleep disturbances, decreased libido, headache or migraine, cardiometabolic disturbances (such as high blood pressure), weight gain, and loss of bone mineral density.

These symptoms can be distressing and can affect women's quality of life.

Why complementary therapies?

Some women prefer to use complementary therapies alongside conventional treatment, or instead of it, due to side effects of menopausal hormone therapy.

Other women cannot use MHT because of other medical conditions, such as breast cancer, or being at risk of venous thromboembolism (blood clots in the deep veins of the leg, which can be fatal if they travel to the lungs).

But what does the evidence say about complementary therapies used in menopause?

The brain science of perimenopause can change everything for women 'Brain fog' during perimenopause is real, and it can disrupt women's lives and careers.

Earlier this year, we and our colleagues published a large review to draw together the evidence. We analysed 158 clinical trials and systematic reviews conducted in women over 40. These studies looked at 86 complementary therapies, such as acupuncture, Chinese herbal medicine, vitamin and nutrient supplements, and mind-body approaches.

Most studies were of low or very low quality. This could be because they included a small number of participants, were not double-blinded (when neither the participants nor the researchers knew which people were given which therapy) and sometimes did not use placebos.

So clinicians don't have sufficient evidence to recommend them.

Now, the detail

Most studies in the review asked women to report the frequency and severity of their symptoms. Some used questionnaires covering a range of symptoms to give an overall menopause score. Others just asked about hot flushes.

Here are some of the findings.

Black cohosh is a flowering plant that improves overall menopausal scores, and hot flushes. Studies found benefits when taken from four to 52 weeks. Women took different products containing black cohosh, on its own or with other herbs. None of these studies reported serious side effects.

Isoflavones also known as phytoestrogens are found in soy and other legumes, and mimic oestrogen in the body. Soy-derived isoflavones improve hot flushes as well as overall menopausal scores. However in the same study, red clover-derived isoflavones did not reduce hot flushes. Side effects to isoflavones are generally mild and improve quickly without needing medical intervention.

Our ability to make vitamin D from sunlight reduces as we get older. In women, this decline starts at about the same time as menopause. For reducing the risk of fracture, women who have diagnosed osteoporosis need to take 800 IU (international units) vitamin D and 1,200 milligram calcium daily under medical supervision. But vitamin D plus calcium are not recommended to women without osteoporosis and without low vitamin D levels. This is because long-term use (over seven years) may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (such as a heart attack).

Isoflavones also known as phytoestrogens are found in soy and other legumes, and mimic oestrogen in the body. (Flickr.)

Chinese herbal medicines can be combinations of multiple herbs (often between five and 20) in a formula. Seventy studies, using a variety of formulas, showed taking Chinese herbal medicines for seven days to three months improved menopausal scores and sleep quality. The most common formula was Suan Zao Ren Tang. Short-term use (up to a year) appears to be safe, but there are no studies looking at its longer-term use.

Another meta-analysis on Chinese herbal medicines using Rehmannia as the main herb found 17 studies. When taken for two weeks to three months there was an improvement in overall menopausal scores. No adverse events were reported.

Acupuncture comes in several forms and you can have it with and without other therapies. We found no evidence to recommend regular acupuncture for hot flushes. Acupuncture with Chinese herbal medicines improves sleep quality, but only in perimenopausal women with insomnia. Electro-acupunture is a form of acupuncture that passes a gentle current between two needles into your skin. It improves hot flushes.

In summary, most treatments included in our review did not show enough evidence to be able to recommend them clinically. Complementary therapies including soy-isoflavones, vitamin D, black cohosh and Chinese herbal medicine may help some menopausal symptoms, but more high-quality research is needed to understand how effective and safe these treatments truly are.

So what should I do?

The International Menopause Society recommends that if women in midlife choose complementary therapies, these should be alongside MHT.

So always talk to your GP about your plans, and only consider using the complementary therapies that have good evidence for the symptoms you currently have. Your GP can help you think about the risks and benefits for you, and help you make a decision based on the best available scientific evidence.

A healthy lifestyle — including eating well, staying active, looking after your mental wellbeing, getting restorative sleep, maintaining healthy relationships, and avoiding drugs and alcohol — are all important in menopause care.

These are linked with benefits including fewer hot flushes, a healthier weight, a lower risk of heart disease and diabetes, and a lower risk of falls and fractures.

Complementary therapies should not replace these fundamental lifestyle habits.

Evangeline Mantzioris is program director of nutrition and food sciences and an accredited practising dietitian at Adelaide University; Alison Maunder is a postdoctoral research fellow at the National Institute of Complementary Medicine at Western Sydney University; and Carolyn Ee is an associate professor of cancer survivorship and primary care at the Caring Futures Institute at Flinders University and Western Sydney University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: World Cup fans to be charged $200 for 15 minute train trip
World.content:
Sky-high ticket prices for matches will not be the only thing emptying the wallets of football fans attending the FIFA World Cup at some US venues this year.

Fans trying to get to New Jersey's MetLife Stadium from New York City can expect to shell out $209 for a round-trip train fare for each match, transportation officials have confirmed.

That is nearly 18 times the regular $18 fare for the roughly 15-minute, 14-kilometre ride from Manhattan's Penn Station to the stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. On-site parking will not be available for most fans, so New Jersey officials anticipate about 40,000 fans will use mass transit for each match.

The home stadium for both the NFL's New York Giants and New York Jets is set to host eight World Cup matches, including the tournament final on July 20 (AEST). Group stage matches for soccer powerhouses Brazil, France, Germany and England, along with other nations, begin June 13.

New Jersey officials said the increase was necessary to cover the cost of hosting the World Cup on its return to the US for the first time since 1994.

NJ Transit says the increase is due to a need to "recoup our costs". (AP: Seth Wenig)

NJ Transit officials said they planned to spend $86.4 million transporting fans to and from the stadium over the duration of the tournament. Outside grants had defrayed only $19.5 million of those anticipated expenses. A fare increase was needed to cover the rest, according to NJ Transit president and chief executive Kris Kolluri.

"This isn't price gouging," he told reporters on Friday local time.

"We're literally trying to recoup our costs."

FIFA provides more expensive World Cup tickets After a backlash over ticket prices, FIFA puts up a new option for fans — and it is more expensive.

Governor Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, called on FIFA to cover the transportation costs.

"If it won't, we will not be subsidising World Cup ticket holders on the backs of New Jerseyans who rely on NJ TRANSIT every day," she said in a statement.

Taking public transit to World Cup matches in Boston's suburbs will also be costly.

Express buses from various locations to Gillette Stadium, home of the NFL's New England Patriots, will cost $132, officials announced this week.

And thousands of fans have already snapped up $111 round-trip train tickets from Boston to the commuter rail station near the stadium. That is four times the $28 riders are normally charged for a round-trip ticket during game days and other special events at Gillette, which is located in Foxborough, a town some 48 kilometres from Boston.

Other World Cup host cities have pledged to keep their transit fares unchanged, noting that the US government has provided some $139 million in transit grants to host cities to provide enhanced bus and rail service.

FIFA has bristled at the suggestion that it should cover the transit costs, noting that the agreements signed with World Cup host cities back in 2018 called for free transportation for fans to all matches. It also argued that no other major event held at MetLife has been required to pay for fan transportation.

PSG fans at MetLife Stadium during the 2025 Club World Cup. (AP: Adam Hunger)

"We are quite surprised by the NJ Governor's approach today on fan transportation," the organisation said in a statement, as news reports of the reported fare began to circulate.

"FIFA worked for years with host cities on transportation and mobility plans, including advocating for millions of dollars in federal funding to support host cities for transportation."

Alternatives to taking the train to MetLife Stadium will also be pricey.

Shuttle buses with a capacity for about 10,000 riders will set off from the midtown Manhattan bus terminal and other locations for $111 round trip.

Some 5,000 parking spots at the nearby American Dream Mall are also being sold in advance, currently priced at $313.

MetLife Stadium has a huge parking lot, but for World Cup matches much of that space is being used for a fan village, shuttle buses, a staging area and FIFA staff, officials said.

AP

World.title: Producer backs pitch for major film studio in Port Kembla
World.content:
Industrial land the size of Sydney's CBD, flanked by the beach and bush, has emerged as a potential new home for New South Wales' second major film studio.

The NSW government has put $100 million on the table to build a film studio in Sydney, but advocates in the Illawarra region have argued Port Kembla, an hour-and-a-half drive down the M1, would be the ideal setting.

The plan has the backing of one of Australia's most prominent producers.

"Whether it's bushland, beaches, suburbia, Wollongong canvases a really wide range of physical environments to be able to pick from," Ian Collie said.

Wollongong is renowned for its unique landscape and landmarks like the Sea Cliff Bridge. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Mr Collie has produced some of Australia's most popular TV shows, including Rake, Jack Irish and Colin From Accounts.

"There are some cost-saving measures with Wollongong being so close to Sydney, allowing cast and crew to move quite freely between the two," he said.

" I think it's a bit of a win-win. "

The state government wants to supplement Disney Studios in Moore Park by partnering with the private sector to deliver a minimum of six sound stages within 100 kilometres of Sydney.

Ian Collie is a film producer and Wombarra property owner. (Supplied: Easy Tiger Productions)

Mr Collie familiarised himself with the Illawarra while filming the TV drama One Night in Wollongong three years ago.

"A lot of NSW-based productions are shot in Sydney, often for economic reasons, but shooting One Night near Thirroul, Scarborough and Coledale just felt so fresh," he said.

" I think we need to expand the regional envelope in terms of the film and TV industry, and the way of doing that is having a studio. "

Studio on steelmaking land

Wollongong councillor Ann Martin and not-for-profit Screen Illawarra are lobbying for a film lot to be built on land owned by steelmaker BlueScope.

BlueScope is redeveloping surplus Port Kembla land. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The Port Kembla Land Transformation Precinct will see 200 hectares of land rezoned.

NSW TAFE and manufacturing companies have already expressed an interest, but film advocates argue the site is perfect for screen productions.

Cr Martin said a film studio would be an opportunity to reshape Port Kembla's future as more than just a steel city.

Wollongong council has supported Ann Martin's motion to advocate for a film studio. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

"The dynamism of [Bluescope's] transformation project should not just be about conventional manufacturing jobs. It should also be about creative jobs," she said.

"Otherwise, it's going to end up another industrial site."

Criteria adjusted for Wollongong

Expressions of interest (EOI) in the NSW government's search for a second film studio close in May, with three locations in Western Sydney already earmarked.

Volunteer-run organisation Screen Illawarra successfully advocated to have the EOI criteria for the location extended from within 35 kilometres of Sydney's CBD to 100 kilometres to make Wollongong bids eligible.

Abandoned railway tunnels in the Illawarra escarpment feature in a Planet of the Apes film. (Supplied: Emily Parisi)

Screen Illawarra chair Nick Bolton said the organisation had been lobbying BlueScope to incorporate a studio into its redevelopment well before the EOI opened.

"We brought Netflix, Amazon, Warner Brothers and the BBC down for a familiarisation tour run by Destination Wollongong and Investor Wollongong 16 months ago and sent all their details to BlueScope," he said.

Bluescope representatives joined a visit to Disney Studios at Moore Park in January.

Nick Bolton says Port Kembla ticks all the boxes for the state's second major film studio. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Mr Bolton said a film studio was flagged as a redevelopment option during a BlueScope community and industry briefing in 2023.

"That's why we've advocated for the last 18 months. There was interest there," he said.

'No proposal'

Despite movie studio representatives visiting the region, BlueScope said it had not received a proposal from a film company.

BlueScope head of property development Michael Yiend said in a statement that the company would not be submitting a bid, but it remained open to receiving detailed proposals for commercially viable opportunities for its land transformation.

"BlueScope is a steelmaker, not a filmmaker," he said.

Government, Screen Illawarra, University of Wollongong and BlueScope representatives toured Disney Studios at Moore Park. (Supplied: Alison Byrnes)

Mr Bolton and Mr Collie said they were hopeful an interested party would come forward before the EOI closed next month.

"We can see a really bright future here, and we want to make it happen," Mr Bolton said.

World.title: Not all city suburbs have NBN access and it isn't by accident. Here's why
World.content:
In 2026, access to fast and reliable internet is something most Australians take for granted.

Gone are the days of dial-up internet that scrambled the phone line and USB 4G dongles holding only a few gigabytes at a time.

That's largely because of the introduction of the National Broadband Network (NBN) in 2009, which, despite its own rollout controversies, was ultimately a turning point in the country's access to the internet.

But 17 years after it was first announced, not all Australians — even in metropolitan areas — receive access to the NBN.

And that isn't because of a delay; it's by legislative design.

When the NBN was first announced by the Rudd Labor government, the public was told 90 per cent of "all Australian homes, schools and workplaces" would be connected to fibre-optic broadband services.

Kevin Rudd inspects cabling to be used for the NBN, during the 2013 election campaign. (Getty: Stefan Postles)

But a detail lost on many is that the promise did not specifically commit to giving access to the publicly owned NBN — only to a fibre-optic broadband network generally, which in some areas only includes private providers.

While it may sound like a technicality when the NBN is the default primary provider, it means hundreds of thousands of Australians are limited to private providers because of where they live, receiving services that aren't always to the standard of the NBN.

'Patchy' internet service in the digital age

Opticomm customers struggle to get compensation for outages Opticomm customers say they struggle to receive compensation for the sometimes monthly internet outages they experience.

Over the last several months, the ABC has heard from dozens of customers of major private network provider Opticomm — which services half a million properties across Australia — who say they experience recurring and prolonged outages, sometimes lasting from one day to two weeks.

Customers say those outages are a huge disruption to their day-to-day lives, leaving them unable to work from home, access online banking or stream entertainment and news — with some having separately lost access to free-to-air television because of changes to Opticomm technology.

Many of those affected are resorting to using and even paying extra for mobile data.

Dozens of Opticomm customers have told the ABC they have experienced significant issues with their internet. (ABC News Graphic: Randi Dahnial)

The chief executive of the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network, Carol Bennett says Opticomm's service, which she describes as "at best patchy", raises significant issues for their customers in the digital age.

"[Unreliable internet] stops [people] from working, from getting access to health services, government services, and really it is an economic and social disadvantage to people when they can't access their internet," she said.

Add the layer that Opticomm typically operates in newly developed, greenfield suburbs — which offer more affordable housing — and the inequality deepens, with access to internet coming down to the luck of the postcode draw.

Carol Bennett says Opticomm's "patchy" service is having real impacts on its customers. (ABC News: John Gunn)

In a statement, Opticomm told the ABC it was investing in infrastructure to "improve [its] network throughout Australia".

Federal Communications Minister Anika Wells previously would not comment on whether the government would act on the issue, with her office only saying they "expect parity between private wholesalers and the NBN".

But as complaints have continued to flow from Opticomm customers to local MPs, industry regulators and consumer peak bodies, this month the minister's office said the relevant department was "considering options" under the legislation.

Anika Wells's office says her government expects "parity between private wholesalers and the NBN". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

For consumers, the hope would be that the options on the table will result in genuinely better service.

But it will be no small task for the government, because according to experts, real change would be reliant on significant reform being made to the Telecommunications Act.

The expectation vs reality gap on what defines good internet

In its current form, the Act only lays out a handful of standards around access to the services provided by statutory infrastructure providers like the NBN and Opticomm.

These standards include that infrastructure providers must connect and supply broadband internet in areas where they operate and offer peak speeds of at least 25Mbps for downloads and 5Mbps for uploads (though the NBN has additional speed targets to this).

There are also standards additional to the Act that dictate infrastructure providers must notify customers of outages — with Opticomm fined $150,000 in June last year for falling short.

Some Opticomm customers have reported experiencing almost monthly outages. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

But industry experts say what the Act fails to do is set a standard for internet service quality that most consumers would consider a given.

As a result, in a report published in September last year, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) recommended the government introduce "clear and enforceable service quality standards" into the Act, including around lag times and how often pages and information fail to load.

Without those additions, customers facing poor service will continue to be left with little access to compensation because, ultimately, the regulator can't enforce rules that don't exist.

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert says access to reliable internet "shouldn't depend on your postcode or which provider you use". (Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman)

One rule for the NBN, another for private providers

For the NBN, the gaps in the Act are papered over by separate legislation that calls on the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to play a significant role in its regulation.

It's an extra layer of regulation that private providers don't face, meaning the NBN is in a league of its own.

As a publicly owned company, the NBN is held to a higher standard than private infrastructure providers. (Supplied)

Ms Bennett argues the ACCC could take steps to regulate private providers like Opticomm if enough complaints are made, and the ACCC has even said it is "currently considering" whether its existing regulation of the private broadband sector should be adjusted.

But even if that change is made, it's fair to say it would be a bureaucratic bandaid solution that doesn't plug the gaping holes in the Act and allows the government to avoid taking direct responsibility.

And so while the government's statement that it expects parity between the private sector and the NBN is a nice sentiment, it isn't one they have legislated — making it of little help to Australians.

Until that fact changes, advocates agree that many Australians will continue to be left on the back foot in the digital era, and the divide among us will grow.

World.title: Frustrated parents look to enforce 'ineffective' social media ban
World.content:
When Australia banned social media access for under-16-year-olds late last year, it was a world-leading move.

The new laws were a response to growing concerns about the negative mental health impacts of the online world on young minds.

But four months on, many parents remain frustrated that their children are still able to access platforms such as Snapchat, Instagram and TikTok.

The calls come as the eSafety Commission announced last month it would move from a compliance monitoring position, to one of enforcement.

Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube are being investigated for "potential noncompliance" with the social media ban for under 16s. (ABC News)

Parent Felicity Williams said she has done everything in her power to uphold the ban for her child, but has found it "impossible" due to a lack of regulatory support.

" In reality, nothing is happening on the ground. It's still being left to parents to enforce. "

Despite the strictest parental controls, Ms Williams' 14-year-old has been able to download the messaging app Snapchat.

"I believe she clicked 'allow' when she's been face-timing her grandparents," she said.

Ms Williams deleted the app, blocked access to it on her home internet and reported the breach to Snapchat.

Felicity Williams has written to Snapchat to remind them of their legal responsibility to keep under 16s off its platform. (Supplied: Felicity Williams)

The social media company said it would investigate, but would not inform Ms Williams of the outcome, "to protect the privacy of the account holder".

Despite her actions, her daughter again gained access to the platform after re-downloading the app through iCloud, where she didn't need parental permission.

Ms Williams emailed Snapchat again.

"I have informed you that an underage child is using your app," she wrote.

"You are aware of it and have done nothing to prevent it, except tell me to use parent controls.

"Under Australian legislation, Snapchat has legal responsibilities to stamp this out," she told the company.

Ban 'ineffective'

Ms Williams did not stop there.

She had a lengthy phone call with Apple, but was unable to have the app removed from her daughter's iCloud.

The teen social media ban explained Here's everything you need to know about the social media ban.

She remains worried about the addictive nature of social media and the risk of online bullying and feels frustrated that in the App Store, Snapchat remains listed for 13-plus age groups.

"It kind of feels like it's a movie that's been incorrectly rated," she said.

Her experience led to her to write to the federal Communications Minister, Anika Wells, her local member of parliament, Matt Thistlethwaite, and the eSafety commissioner.

Ms Williams said the responses she received have been unsatisfactory.

She says she feels "very frustrated and very let down" and describes the ban as "ineffective" and "extremely difficult to police".

Tech companies 'taking the mickey'

Greg Attwells campaigned for Australia's social media law changes through his for-profit company 36 Months.

He sympathises with parents who hoped the law change would keep their kids off social media.

"It sucks," he said.

"It does feel like the platforms haven't complied fully with the new laws and are taking the mickey".

Greg Attwells petitioned the federal government to introduce the age-restricting laws. (ABC News)

At the same time, Mr Attwells said he had also heard from families where the new rules have worked.

"We've been getting reports from parents saying, 'I'm coming home from work and six kids are out in the backyard, playing backyard cricket under sprinklers … [with] phones inside for hours kind of not being looked at or touched'," he said.

With other countries around the world working to establish a similar ban, Mr Attwells believes tech companies are "incentivised to make the rollout [in Australia] as wobbly as possible".

On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron announced a bill, inspired by Australia's social media ban, would go before the parliament.

Move to 'enforcement stance'

A recent report on the issue by the eSafety Commission concluded that platform pathways for parents to report underage users were ineffective and inaccessible.

It also raised compliance concerns.

Five social media companies investigated over response to teen ban Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube are being investigated for potential noncompliance with the ban, almost four months after the laws came into force.

In a blog post, eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said the body would be "moving from a compliance monitoring to an enforcement stance".

"We will not hesitate to take enforcement action where appropriate," a spokesperson said.

The eSafety Commission report found that while social media account ownership for 8—15-year-olds had dropped from 49.7 per cent to 31.3 per cent since the laws came into effect, Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube would be under investigation for potentially failing to comply with the ban.

It identified a range of what it called poor practices that encouraged children and teens to access the platforms.

If found to be non-compliant, the platforms could face infringement notices and civil penalties.

The eSafety Commission's website provides advice on the topic for parents.

Teen retains access despite ban

Parent Alexis Theodorou said since the ban, nothing had changed for her 14-year-old son. She feels the tech companies have not taken it seriously.

"He hasn't been removed from any of the social media platforms that he uses," she said.

"It seems to me a bit optimistic to think that all the social media companies would just go, 'OK, we'll just get rid of all the under-16s off social media'.

" I don't think it was ever going to be that simple. "

Alexis Theodorou wants her son removed from social media platforms. (ABC News)

Ms Theodorou wishes the ban had come in years earlier, when her son was younger, "as I would have felt more supported in delaying his use of social media".

" Once your child has a phone, unless you are tech savvy and on top of all the parental controls, it's difficult to know everything they are doing. "

Younger users linked to higher depression rates

A recent study of young people in the United States looked at links between the age of smartphone acquisition and depression, obesity and insufficient sleep.

Lead researcher Ran Barzilay, a child and adolescent psychiatrist from the Children's Hospital in Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania, said while the study did not look specifically at social media use, a child's age at smartphone acquisition was a good place to start for information on phone use and its impact on young minds.

US-based academic Ran Barzilay looked at the link between phone use and its impact on young minds. (Supplied: Ran Barzilay)

Of the roughly 10,000 participants, 6,739 had a smartphone at age 12.

"We found that on average, kids with smartphones had more chances of meeting the criteria for depression, obesity and insufficient sleep at age 12," Associate Professor Barzilay said.

He said the link was stronger for kids who had received a smartphone earlier.

"For every year younger of smartphone acquisition, there [is] around a 10 per cent increase in the chance of the kid having obesity or insufficient sleep at age 12," he said.

Associate Professor Barzilay said further studies would look at the effects of delaying smartphone use. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Children who did not have a smartphone at the age of 12, but acquired one by the age of 13, had a 50 per cent chance of experiencing mental health problems or reporting insufficient sleep compared with those who remained without a smartphone.

Associate Professor Barzilay said further studies were underway, particularly looking at the impacts of delaying smartphone use.

"I'm not saying [smartphones are] just bad, to the same extent I'm not saying it's all good. It has both sides to it," he said.

"But it's very important to take the decision thoughtfully and acknowledge that this decision has implications for the kid's health."

Messy start to ban

Federal Minister for Communications Anika Wells said social media platforms were pushing back against the ban, and she expected the implementation of the new laws to be "untidy on the way through".

"Big tech is using every play in the playbook," she said.

"They are worried that now more than a dozen countries have followed Australia and that these laws are rolling out in different places across the world.

"But we will keep fighting for you against the richest, most resourced companies in the world who want to use your children's data for revenue.

" If eSafety finds these platforms have systemically failed to uphold their legal obligations, I expect the commissioner to throw the book at them. "

Anika Wells says she will support the findings of the eSafety Commissioner. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

A Snapchat spokesperson said the service remained committed to implementing reasonable steps under the legislation and supporting its underlying goal of improving online safety for young Australians.

"We have locked 450,000 accounts and continue to lock more every day."

The spokesperson said the company had engaged constructively with the eSafety commissioner on "this new and untested law" and had taken strong steps to prevent underage users from having Snapchat accounts, "recognising that it will be iterative and will continue to strengthen our approach".

Social media company Meta — the owner of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Threads — did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: New scooters and e-bikes have arrived in Canberra. Here's what that means
World.content:
Shared e-bikes have been introduced to Canberra's streets for the first time, along with new e-scooters, as Lime starts operating in the capital in partnership with the ACT government.

The new green-coloured fleet includes 1,200 e-scooters and 300 e-bikes, spread across the city's town centres, and takes over from Neuron's orange scooters after it left Canberra's shared micromobility market.

"Shared e‑scooters and e‑bikes make active travel and public transport easier and more appealing, reducing the need to rely on a car for every trip," City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said.

" Expanding the program to include shared e‑bikes gives the community more choice and makes active travel more accessible. "

Tighter speed limits and regulations have been brought in as shared e-bikes enter Canberra's streets. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

How do Lime e-scooters and e-bikes work?

Users must download the Lime app to access the devices and scan a QR code to activate an electric scooter or bike to start riding.

Prices are dictated by the length of time the device is in use, and the charge goes through once the journey is completed.

Shared e-bikes are new to Canberra, while shared e-scooters have been a presence for six years. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

The app includes instructions on how to park and how to navigate safely around pedestrians, doorways and sidewalks.

The devices are available to use in the city centre, Belconnen, Fyshwick, Gungahlin, Majura, Molonglo Valley, Tuggeranong, Weston Creek and Woden.

Coroner calls for more e-scooter safety awareness A coroner calls for increased public safety campaigns after a 14-year-old boy died after colliding with a ute while riding an e-scooter in regional Victoria.

"At the moment we have scooters and bikes in every major district and over time we will work with Lime to expand where they are accessible," Kira Cox of the City and Environment Directorate said.

" So right now, regardless of whether you're in Tuggeranong or the inner city, you will be able to find a bike or a scooter. "

Under its agreement with the government, Lime is allowed around 3,000 devices.

Lime's scooters have the potential to travel up to 59 kilometres, depending on factors such as elevation, and e-bikes have a range of 64km.

The bikes also include a basket and Ms Cheyne said they had been designed to suit both male and female riders.

What are the rules for riders?

Lime e-bike and scooter users must be at least 16 years of age, with only one person permitted on a device at any time — passengers are not allowed.

Users must also wear a helmet, give way to pedestrians, and ensure they park off pathways and away from stairs, ramps, bus stops, light rail stops and entry or exits to buildings.

The Lime app functions similarly to other apps like Uber. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

While helmets are provided, users can bring their own helmets instead, and the company keeps a record of helmet use.

E-scooters can be used on footpaths, shared paths and nature strips, but can only be used on roads or bicycle lanes if there is no available footpath, shared path or nature strip.

E-bike users can ride anywhere that a pushbike can travel.

It is illegal to travel on a scooter or e-bike faster than 15km/h on footpaths and 25km/h on shared paths and bike paths.

If a crash occurs and the rider is at fault, they are held liable in the same way they would be using a private device.

"So riders ride at their own risk and if they crash into somebody, and they do so because they are behaving badly or against the road rules, then that is absolutely a risk that they are taking personally," Ms Cox said.

Lime e-bikes can be used by anyone aged 16 or older. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

The devices are not permitted on buses or light rail, with users encouraged to take them to and from public transport.

If one is left in an area where it is not permitted, the company is expected to take action, Ms Cheyne said.

"And if there are areas where enforcement needs to be stepped up or tightened, then that's a conversation, of course, that we can have," she said.

How will Lime scooters and e-bikes be regulated?

Ms Cheyne said automatic speed limits were in place to help protect both riders and pedestrians in busy areas.

Device speeds are automatically reduced to 10km/h at priority crossings and 15km/h in congested areas.

Lime uses geofencing technology to enforce the speed limits, and no-ride zones have been established in different parts of the city.

"Recently here in the city we've been able to geofence some locations and require the scooters to go slower than their usual speed or their maximum speed which is 25 kilometres an hour," Ms Cheyne said.



"[So] where we've had a bit more of a concentration of people moving to an area, like outside Mooseheads for example."

Tara Cheyne and Will Peters launch Canberra's new fleet of shared e-bikes and e-scooters. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

Ms Cheyne added that the app included clear instructions on how to use the e-scooters and e-bikes safely.

She said there was also not as much concern in the Canberra community about the devices as had been reported in other jurisdictions.

"Safety underpins everything we do," Lime's head of Asia-Pacific Will Peters said.

"We're proud to become part of Canberra's transport mix and to offer residents and visitors another easy way to get around the city."

What has been learned from previous operators?

Ms Cheyne said the government had learned lessons from years of Beam and Neuron operating shared scooters in the ACT.

In September 2024, the ACT government ordered Beam to remove its scooters from Canberra streets after it was revealed the company manipulated data about its fleet.

The company had been outside permit limits by having more scooters on the road than were allowed.

Ms Cheyne said Beam's transgressions had informed the new partnership with Lime.

Lime e-scooters and e-bikes are not permitted on light rail or buses. (ABC News: Niki Burnside)

"It has been a learning in terms of having a program manager, and we have a dedicated program manager for the arrangement with Lime, and this means that government and the provider are working effectively hand in glove," she said.

"But it also means that in the permit that we've provided for Lime to operate, there are conditions that Lime needs to act within.

"There's been a really, really rigorous process for Lime to be selected as a provider on the ACT and we're really looking forward to a productive relationship over the next few years."

World.title: Man hospitalised after machete attack at Melbourne shopping mall
World.content:
An 18-year-old man has been hospitalised after a being attacked with machetes by a group of men at a popular shopping strip in Melbourne's south-east.

Police say the victim was approached by approximately 12 men while sitting outside a business at Eaton Mall in Oakleigh about 7:45pm on Friday night, before a fight broke out.

Investigators say the men were wearing balaclavas and that at least two of them produced machetes before allegedly assaulting the victim.

"A physical altercation occurred before the group fled the scene on foot," a Victoria Police spokesman said.

"The male was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries."

A 16-year-old boy was also assaulted in the attack, but was not injured.

Detectives say the attack is being treated as a targeted incident and that the two parties were known to each other.

Patrols in the area will be increased today, in a move Victoria Police said was designed to "provide reassurance to the community".

No arrests have been made.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has dashcam, CCTV footage, or has information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online.

World.title: Long before Dezi Freeman, other criminals hid along the Upper Murray
World.content:
It's a region known for its rugged beauty, occasional natural disasters and the folklore of Australia's great cattlemen.

Now, north-east Victoria's Upper Murray is forever linked to the tale of Dezi Freeman and his seven-month run from police.

The manhunt for the police killer ended on a cool morning in Thologolong, 76 kilometres upstream from Wodonga.

But Freeman is not the only fugitive to take shelter in these hills.

Picnic shooting

"In the early stages of colonial history, this place was like the Wild West," according to Walwa resident Janice Newnham.

The local author and amateur historian has extensively researched some of the skeletons in the Upper Murray's closet, as the foundation for her latest novel.

Janice Newnham has extensively researched the area's history of violent fugitives. (ABC News: Rachel Carbonell)

One of those is the tale of Claude Batson, who opened fire on a group of picnickers on the banks of Jingellic Creek more than a century ago.

A skilled marksman, Batson killed one of the picnic-goers and seriously injured three others.

After the shooting in February 1924, he fled into the hills above Jingellic in southern New South Wales.

Claude Batson, pictured at the time of his arrest, was featured in a newspaper article in The Argus in 1949 with the headline "The Sniper of Jingellic Creek". (Supplied: National Library of Australia)

"[It's] easy to get lost in, lots of trees and bushes and shrubbery to hide in amongst, and he knew all the crevasses and caves up there," Newnham said.

"Batson had a bit of a chip on his shoulder … and a lot of trauma in his past," she said.

"He just cracked."

He was eventually captured after a six-day manhunt through steep and rocky terrain.

The rugged terrain of the Upper Murray during the January 2026 bushfires. (Supplied: Forest Fire Management Victoria)

Batson spent the rest of his days in an asylum on the NSW Central Coast, after the court declared him unfit to stand trial.

It's not clear what sparked the shooting spree — but Newnham's research suggested Batson's attempts to create a rabbit poison may have been involved.

"He was experimenting with different types of gases and poisons and chemicals … he potentially poisoned himself, and [that] might've sent him into a state of derangement," Newnham said.

High country crime

More than half a century later, police officer Patrick Brear relocated to nearby Wodonga — looking for "a bit of R and R".

The 73-year-old didn't get his wish.

"On my first night, we had a stabbing in Mitta and things didn't really slow down from there," he said.

In the summer of 1984, Mr Brear, then a detective senior constable, got a call alerting him to the presence of a heavily armed man near Nariel, south of Corryong.

Andrew Joseph Medlock had kidnapped and terrorised a couple at a farmhouse in the NSW town of Woomargama a few days earlier.

Weapons were found in the vehicle Andrew Joseph Medlock was driving. (ABC News: Sarah Krieg)

After stealing their car and guns, he crossed into Victoria and headed for the hills.

But he ran out of fuel, and police were dispatched after a dog trapper came across Medlock and his weapons arsenal stranded on a hillside.

Mr Brear headed up the valley with three NSW special weapons operatives from Albury.

"It was somewhat of a dilemma as to whether we should act immediately, or give it 24 hours to establish a proper and fully resourced operation … to arrest who we already knew was an extremely dangerous person," Mr Brear said.

One newspaper clipping shows police arresting Andrew Joseph Medlock in the Upper Murray. (ABC News: Sarah Krieg)

In the end, Mr Brear approached the vehicle disguised as the dog trapper.

Unarmed, he was just a few metres away from the business end of one of Medlock's weapons when his colleagues swooped, arresting the would-be gunman before he could fire.

"Undoubtedly, had he been able to fuel up and get back down into the farm valleys … we can only guess what might have happened," Mr Brear said.

A good spot to go off-grid

By nature, the Upper Murray is a decent hiding spot.

There are hidden bush tracks, difficult terrain and neighbours can be kilometres away.

Drone pictures of the region show how hilly and remote the area is. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

That isolation has been attractive in the past — and in recent times, to a fugitive like Dezi Freeman.

"People keep to themselves up here … so you can see why it sort of happened," said Thologolong local Dean McKimmie.

During his time as a detective, Mr Brear investigated other illegal activities in the area, including along the Firebrace Track, which runs south of the Mt Lawson State Park.

Dense forest surrounds the property where Dezi Freeman was shot dead by police. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"There are lots of little communities set up along that particular ridge," he said.

"Some people use them for holiday shacks … [but] we found that people of a less-than-honest means were using the area to dump vehicles and grow drugs … and just generally hide within the trees hoping to not alert neighbours or the police," he said.

Mr Brear said people should not judge the region by recent headlines — or past police operations.

"I wouldn't want to suggest that this [area] is a Mecca for miscreants to flock to, to hide from police," he said.

But it certainly has its advantages — and locals know there are areas that seldom see visitors.

"The bush is quite dense … there's plenty of places to get lost, be hidden, evade the law," Newnham said.

First, we called for the unconditional, unrestricted, and immediate re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz. The right of transit passage without restrictions or tolls is the bedrock of international trade. Freedom of navigation means navigation must be free. We therefore welcome the announcement today that the Strait will re-open and underline that this must endure. The disruption to global energy security, supply chains, and economic and financial stability must end, for the benefit of communities right across the world, in particular for the poorest and most vulnerable. We committed to coordinating our economic responses and to avoid protectionist actions.

Second, we confirmed our support for the vital work of the International Maritime Organisation to ensure the safety of seafarers and vessels. Third, France and the United Kingdom confirmed that they are establishing an independent and strictly defensive multinational mission to protect merchant vessels, reassure commercial shipping operators, and conduct mine clearance operations as soon as conditions permit following a sustainable ceasefire agreement.

World.title: An activist’s bid for Broncos to oust News Corp as major shareholder
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandNRL 2026 An activist’s bid for Broncos to oust News Corp as major shareholder Cameron Atfield April 18, 2026 — 6:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Shareholder activist Stephen Mayne has launched a bid to join the Brisbane Broncos board, with one aim in mind – the removal of News Corp as the club’s majority shareholder. Mayne said the US-based media company’s 24-year grip on the club represented an unacceptable conflict of interest and was out of step with Australian sporting traditions. Speaking ahead of the Broncos’ upcoming annual general meeting, at which he will self-nominate for the board, Mayne said News Corp’s near-70 per cent holding in the club was an “anomaly” that would not be tolerated elsewhere in Australian sport. Shareholder activist Stephen Mayne is seeking a seat on the Brisbane Broncos board - and wants Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp out of the club. Jamie Brown “The biggest newspaper in Queensland owns and controls the biggest sporting team in Queensland,” he told this masthead.



“That is a massive conflict of interest to start with.” News Corp, controlled by Rupert Murdoch and headquartered in New York, has owned a majority stake in the Broncos since 2002. It previously held stakes in other sporting teams, including the Melbourne Storm and the Los Angeles Dodgers, but exited those investments years ago. News Corp’s Broncos ownership was “the last hangover” of the Super League wars, Mayne said, and while private ownership was common in American sports, Australia had traditionally favoured member-owned or not-for-profit structures – particularly in rugby league and Australian Rules football. “You wouldn’t let an American billionaire come in and buy Collingwood,” he said. “Everyone would say that’s outrageous. Yet here we have an American-based billionaire effectively controlling the most valuable NRL club.”



Mayne, the founder of news website Crikey, said the problem was not private ownership itself, but concentrated control. “At the moment, the Broncos have around 1200 shareholders but only one of them controls the club,” he said. “That’s inappropriate for an institution of this size and significance.” The Murdochs’ assocation with the Broncos goes back decades: Lachlan Murdoch pictured with Gorden Tallis at Suncorp Stadium in 2004. Jonathan Wood/Getty Images But Mayne conceded his candidature for the Broncos board was largely symbolic, given News Corp’s voting power.



“I can’t get elected because News Corp will vote against me,” he said. “That’s the whole point I’m making – it’s effectively a gerrymander that would make Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen blush.” Mayne said his campaign focused on two reforms: encouraging News Corp to sell down its stake and pushing the Broncos to adopt hybrid annual general meetings, allowing online participation. “There are more than 200 Australian companies running hybrid AGMs,” he said. “You can watch the Broncos play on your phone, but you can’t watch the AGM on your phone.”



The Broncos now represent the final sports team in Rupert Murdoch’s stable, following the sales of the Melbourne Storm and Los Angeles Dodgers. Rocco Fazzari Mayne criticised the club’s refusal to allow remote attendance as an attempt to suppress debate. “Transparency and shareholder participation should be non-negotiable in corporate Australia,” he said. Comment has been sought from the Broncos. Mayne said he was unsure whether he would be able to attend the AGM in person, but would have a proxy in the room if he was unable to make the trip.



The Broncos’ notice of meeting was expected to be released to the Australian Stock Exchange shortly, ahead of the AGM scheduled for May 19. Mayne said how the club handled his nomination would be an early test of its governance standards. Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2025 Brisbane Broncos sport fresh rebrand after 25 years “The first test is whether they publish my arguments uncensored,” Mayne said. “That will say a lot about whether this is a fair election.” Longer term, Mayne proposed limits on individual shareholdings as a way to prevent future concentration of power, pointing to precedents in heavily regulated industries such as casinos.



“I don’t see why the same concept shouldn’t apply here,” he said. “Let News Corp sell down over time and move to a model where no one owns more than, say, 5 per cent.” Such a structure, Mayne said, would better reflect the club’s community role and align it with broader Australian sporting values. “This isn’t about nationalising the Broncos or forcing an immediate sale – it’s about starting a debate that everyone’s too scared to have because of the Murdochs’ power,” he said. “Once people point out how abnormal this structure is, the pressure should be on News Corp to voluntarily sell and let the club be controlled by its supporters and shareholders, not one overseas billionaire.”



News Corp did not respond to a request for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The difference between Meghan and Kate has never been greater
World.content:
LifestyleFashionRoyal family The difference between Meghan and Kate has never been greater Damien Woolnough April 18, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

On the final day of her unofficial Australian tour, it was clear that Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has replaced Catherine, Princess of Wales as a commercial fashion force. Expect sales of the blue and white striped $420 shirt from Australian label Matteau, worn by Meghan to Bondi and sailing on Sydney Harbour yesterday, to match those of the $389 khaki mini dress worn on Thursday from Melbourne label Friends With Frank, which (apart from one in an XL) sold out in 24 hours. After 10 outfit changes in four days – fewer than Margot Robbie on a movie press tour and four more than Princess Anne on her official four-day Australian visit in November – Meghan is the closest person to the crown who can drive sales for emerging labels. Meghan’s best looks: Day 4 Meghan in a Matteau striped shirt and Rolla’s jeans with Prince Harry at Bondi Beach. PA Images via Getty Images



Gemma O’Neill with Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, wearing Scanlan Theodore, at the Her Best Life retreat in Coogee. Instagram @herbestlifepod One of Anne’s outfits was a military uniform, so it’s safe to say that she’s in her own style lane. As Catherine enters her queen-in-waiting era, most recently re-wearing a two-year-old Self-Portrait dress to Easter service with the royal family, she has left showcasing the latest on-trend items to her sister-in-law. It’s a style strategy closer to Queen Mary of Denmark who, on her official Australian tour in March, re-wore favourite pieces from her own wardrobe, including a Zimmermann dress from 2022. Meghan’s approach is closer to content creators such as Paris Hilton, who has also partnered with AI shopping platform One Off for a slice of sales. Meghan’s best looks: Day 3



Meghan in the Friends With Frank ‘Anya’ dress and Harry braving a colour clash at Swinburne University. Getty Images Meghan, wearing an Alliance of Moms T-shirt, Rolla’s jeans and Friends With Frank coat and Harry met with Koorie Heritage Trust to discover the Scar Tree Walk by the Yarra River in Melbourne. PA Images via Getty Images After starting the tour wearing a flared Karen Gee dress on a visit to the Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne, Meghan has churned through Australian labels including St Agni, Camilla and Marc, P Johnson, Dissh and Rolla’s. Promoting a label can have a positive effect for a label, like Meghan wearing Karen Gee for the first time on her official tour of Australia in 2018, putting the little-known designer on the map for corporate women around the country. Meghan also helped sales for fledgling Scottish accessories label Strathberry when she carried their handbag in 2017, which is now projected to surpass £100 million ($189 million) in two years.



Meghan’s best looks: Day 1 & 2 Meghan wearing a Matteau shirt and Camilla & Mac skirt, makes her mark on MasterChef, alongside judges Jean-Christophe Novelli, Poh Ling Yeow and Sofia Levin. Ten Meghan wears the suede utility cocoon bomber and matching skirt from St Agni. Getty Images Meghan wears the Priscilla dress by Sydney-based designer Karen Gee at the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne with Prince Harry. AP While Karen Gee is honoured that Meghan chose to wear her label and Friends With Frank founder Julia McCarthy sees Meghan’s endorsement as a career highlight, Australian Fashion Council executive chair Marianne Perkovic warns labels against banking their success on celebrity support.



“It’s no surprise to see Meghan choosing Australian designers as our industry is globally requested for its quality,” Perkovic says. “Designers need to still have good business strategy and not just rely on these moments. “I think about Taylor Swift wearing Dion Lee and that didn’t help that brand.” Three months after Swift wore one of Lee’s corset tops, the business entered voluntary administration. Lee has since returned with the provocative label Haelo. We missed out on Meghan wearing one of his sheer corsets with black lace appliqué in Australia. Perhaps her approach to dressing is still slightly different to Paris Hilton. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

Third, France and the United Kingdom confirmed that they are establishing an independent and strictly defensive multinational mission to protect merchant vessels, reassure commercial shipping operators, and conduct mine clearance operations as soon as conditions permit following a sustainable ceasefire agreement.
